Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in La Paz, Bolivia at 2026-11-11 12:27 -04 (UTC-0400) (2026-11-11T16:27:00Z in UTC), at latitude -16.4897 degrees and longitude -68.1193 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 87.281 degrees and its azimuth is 246.697 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 64.177 degrees and its azimuth is 119.602 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 5.54 percent illuminated, 27.157 degrees from the Sun, and 397875.5 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To give you an honest estimate: **No, you will almost certainly not be able to see it.**

Here is the breakdown of why, based on the specific data you provided:

### 1. The "Washout" Factor (Solar Glare)
The biggest obstacle is the Sun's position. At an altitude of **87.281 degrees**, the Sun is nearly at its zenith (directly overhead). Even though the Moon is at an altitude of **64.177 degrees**, it is positioned in the sky during peak daylight hours. 

Because the sky is "bright daylight," the atmosphere is scattering a massive amount of sunlight (Rayleigh scattering). This creates a high "background noise" of brightness. For an object to be visible to the naked eye, it must have enough contrast against the blue of the sky to be distinguished.

### 2. The Phase and Magnitude
The Moon is only **5.54% illuminated**. This means you aren't looking at a bright, white orb; you are looking at a very thin, slender crescent. 
*   A Full Moon has a high enough surface area to reflect enough light to be seen even in daylight.
*   A 5% crescent has very little surface area. It will appear as a tiny sliver of light.

### 3. The Angular Separation
The Moon is only **27.157 degrees** away from the Sun. While this is technically "far enough" for the Moon to be above the horizon, it is close enough that the Moon is still bathed in the intense "glare" of the Sun's proximity. In astronomy, this is often where the Moon is "lost" in the solar glare—it's there, but the surrounding atmosphere is so saturated with light that the faint crescent doesn't stand out.

### 4. The "Ordinary Eyesight" Constraint
Since you are using unaided eyesight, your pupils will be constricted due to the bright daylight. This significantly reduces your ability to pick out low-contrast objects. To see this Moon, you would likely need a pair of binoculars to "isolate" the Moon from the surrounding sky brightness.

### The Verdict
If you were to look toward the azimuth of **119.6 degrees** (East-Southeast), you would see a very bright, washed-out sky. Because the Moon is so thin (5.5%) and the Sun is so high (87°), the Moon will be "drowned out" by the ambient light of the atmosphere.

**Probability of spotting it with the naked eye: < 5%**
